title: Sacrificial System
summary: Leviticus describes different offerings for different purposes. Leviticus 1 gives instructions for a burnt offering; Leviticus 4 addresses purification after certain sins; Leviticus 16 describes the annual Day of Atonement and the cleansing of the sanctuary. Psalm 51 says sacrifice cannot replace a contrite heart, yet it also speaks of right offerings in Jerusalem. Hebrews then argues that Jesus' offering accomplishes what repeated sacrifices could not. These passages are connected, but they should not be flattened into one ritual or one claim about sacrifice.
historical_context: The direct passages include ritual instructions in Leviticus, a penitential psalm, and Hebrews' later theological argument. Leviticus 1 describes the burnt offering, Leviticus 4 addresses purification offerings, and Leviticus 16 sets out a distinct annual rite for the sanctuary and the people. Psalm 51:16-19 rejects sacrifice as a substitute for repentance but still imagines right offerings when Jerusalem is restored. Hebrews 9-10 interprets repeated offerings through its claim about Jesus' once-for-all work. These texts do not by themselves establish that practice remained unchanged across every period of Israel's history.
literary_context: Leviticus gives ritual instructions; Psalm 51 is a prayer of repentance that contrasts sacrifice with a broken and contrite heart while still anticipating offerings; Hebrews 9-10 is an argument about the limits of repeated sacrifice and the significance of Jesus' offering. The change in genre matters: a penitential poem and a New Testament argument do not function as additional ritual rules for Leviticus.
covenantal_significance: The Levitical passages associate offerings with atonement, purification, and the sanctuary's holiness. Psalm 51 insists that ritual cannot stand in for repentance, while Hebrews argues that Jesus' offering brings the lasting access and forgiveness it describes. Each passage explains a different part of the relationship between worship, wrongdoing, and restored life with God.
canonical_role: These passages trace distinct conversations about sacrifice: Leviticus gives instructions for particular offerings, Psalm 51 asks what repentance requires, and Hebrews interprets repeated offerings in relation to Jesus. The differences help readers see how biblical texts reuse sacrificial language while making their own claims about worship and forgiveness.

interpretive_notes.note: Leviticus 1 describes the burnt offering, Leviticus 4 addresses purification offerings, and Leviticus 16 gives a separate annual Day of Atonement rite. The text assigns different roles to these offerings rather than presenting one interchangeable sacrifice.

Psalm 51:16-19 says sacrifice cannot replace a broken and contrite heart, yet it still anticipates right offerings in Jerusalem. Hebrews 9-10 makes a distinct argument that Jesus' offering is once for all; the two passages should not be reduced to a single statement that sacrifice has no value.
